Here are some lesser-known facts about the Biosphere 2, off the top of my head... The structure was based on a sophisticated modular space frame system called Min-A-Max that was developed by architect Peter Pearce and first introduced in the book Structure in Nature as a Strategy for Design by MIT Press. Min-A-Max was one of the most clever space frame and dome systems which also had a simpler complementary system called Universal Node System. Pearce started a short-lived company to manufacture the components for Min-A-Max but could not maintain consistent production as demand for space frame structures went into decline in the late 80s. Everything inside the Biosphere was intended to be non-out-gassing and low toxic as to avoid contamination of the atmosphere and water. So parts of the structure used a unique mineral foam insulation called AirKrete that has the consistency of stale angel's food cake and is so non-toxic you can actually eat it. It's also the most fire-proof insulation commonly available and has been used in the lining of blast furnaces. Unfortunately these precautions failed to take into account the chemical nature of the concrete in the foundation of the structure, which undergoes a slow reaction that can last centuries and contributed greatly to the oxygen depletion problem that troubled the experiment. Other problems included an infiltration of ants whose source couldn't be found. The large opaque dome in the background was the habitat's 'lung'. Connected by an underground tunnel, it contained a large balloon that was used as an atmosphere reserve to moderate shifts in atmosphere between the several biome sections. In one of the controversial events of the experiment, the lung was opened to take in fresh air when the original oxygen supply declined to the point where it became hazardous. After the experiment, the property was sold to a land developer that planned to demolish it and redevelop the space into a housing development but it later went into the hands of the University of Arizona which has used it as a research arboretum while keeping it open for tourists.
